quotes.t: Any time you sincerely want to make a change, the first thing you must do is to raise your standards.
You get what you tolerate.
For changes to be of any true value, they've got to be lasting and consistent.
No tree, it is said, can grow to heaven unless its roots reach down to hell.
A man who has not passed through the inferno of his passions has never overcome them.
The healthy man does not torture others. Generally it is the tortured who turn into torturers.
Bitterness is like cancer. It eats upon the host. But anger is like fire. It burns it all clean.
If you are going to live, leave a legacy. Make a mark on the world that can't be erased.
You can't really know where you are going until you know where you have been.
Satisfaction lies in the effort, not in the attainment. Full effort is full victory.
Truth stands, even if there be no public support. It is self-sustained.
Nonviolence is a weapon of the strong.
There is no such thing as a moral or an immoral book. Books are well written, or badly written. That is all.
quotes.source: Preface to The Picture of Dorian Gray (1890)

quotes.t: It is only shallow people who do not judge by appearances.
Consistency is the last refuge of the unimaginative.
Indeed it has been said that democracy is the worst form of Government except for all other forms that have been tried from time to time.
quotes.source: Speech to the House of Commons, 11 November 1947

quotes.t: The empires of the future are the empires of the mind.
It is a mistake to look too far ahead. Only one link of the chain of destiny can be handled at a time.
I do not want the peace which passeth understanding, I want the understanding which bringeth peace.
The world is moved along, not only by the mighty shoves of its heroes, but also by the aggregate of tiny pushes of each honest worker.
Death is no more than passing from one room into another.
Do not think dishonestly.
The Way is in training.
You may abandon your own body but you must preserve your honor.
In battle, there are not more than two methods of attack, the direct and the indirect; yet these two in combination give rise to an endless series of maneuvers.
What the ancients called a clever fighter is one who not only wins, but excels in winning with ease.
Energy may be likened to the bending of a crossbow; decision, to the releasing of a trigger.
The more we come out and do good to others, the more our hearts will be purified, and God will be in them.
Ask nothing; want nothing in return. Give what you have to give; it will come back to you, but do not think of that now.
It is our own mental attitude which makes the world what it is for us.
The smallest feline is a masterpiece.
Nothing can be loved or hated unless it is first understood.
Beyond a doubt, truth bears the same relation to falsehood as light to darkness.
Teaching is a very noble profession that shapes the character, caliber, and future of an individual.
For great men, religion is a way of making friends; small people make religion a fighting tool.
Do not take rest after your first victory because if you fail in second, more lips are waiting to say that your first victory was just luck.
You are responsible for your life. You can't keep blaming somebody else for your dysfunction.
Think like a queen. A queen is not afraid to fail. Failure is another stepping stone to greatness.
We can't become what we need to be by remaining what we are.
In the long run, we shape our lives, and we shape ourselves. The process never ends until we die. And the choices we make are ultimately our own responsibility.
To handle yourself, use your head; to handle others, use your heart.
If life were predictable it would cease to be life, and be without flavor.
I must follow the people. Am I not their leader?
Assassination has never changed the history of the world.
Time is precious, but truth is more precious than time.
God is dead. God remains dead. And we have killed him.
And if you gaze for long into an abyss, the abyss gazes also into you.
There is always some madness in love. But there is also always some reason in madness.
I have cherished the ideal of a democratic and free society in which all persons live together in harmony and with equal opportunities.
Lead from the back, and let others believe they are in front.
If you talk to a man in a language he understands, that goes to his head. If you talk to him in his language, that goes to his heart.
I have made this letter longer than usual because I lack the time to make it shorter.
Reason's last step is the recognition that there are an infinite number of things which are beyond it.
Do you wish people to think well of you? Don't speak well of yourself.
Ah, good taste! What a dreadful thing! Taste is the enemy of creativeness.
Computers are useless. They can only give you answers.
To draw, you must close your eyes and sing.
Let us not be satisfied with just giving money. Money is not enough, money can be got, but they need your hearts to love them.
God doesn't require us to succeed, he only requires that you try.
I have found the paradox, that if you love until it hurts, there can be no more hurt, only more love.
The pupil dilates in darkness and in the end finds light, just as the soul dilates in misfortune and in the end finds God.
There is no sun without shadow, and it is essential to know the night.
Love is real, real is love.
Liberty means responsibility. That is why most men dread it.
I am taught by suffering to endure, and the long years that have grown old with me, and last not least, by true nobility.
Ethics is nothing else than reverence for life.
In war, the moral is to the physical as three is to one.
We can let the circumstances of our lives harden us so that we become increasingly resentful and afraid, or we can let them soften us and make us kinder.
He who is not contented with what he has, would not be contented with what he would like to have.
Better to light a candle than to curse the darkness.
Time is but the stream I go a-fishing in.
When you find your place where you are, practice occurs, actualizing the fundamental point.
The service of India means the service of the millions who suffer.
The madness of love is the greatest of heaven's blessings.
Every man is guilty of all the good he did not do.
We must learn to live together as brothers or perish together as fools.
To live is so startling it leaves little time for anything else.
There are dark shadows on the earth, but its lights are stronger in the contrast.
Hide not your talents, they for use were made. What's a sundial in the shade?
One cannot be always laughing at a man without now and then stumbling on something witty.
All the variety, all the charm, all the beauty of life is made up of light and shadow.
To go wrong in one's own way is better than to go right in someone else's.
Where there's hope, there's life. It fills us with fresh courage and makes us strong again.
quotes.source: The Diary of a Young Girl (1947)

quotes.t: Forgiving is not forgetting; it's actually remembering, remembering and not using your right to hit back.
We write to taste life twice, in the moment and in retrospect.
We have just enough religion to make us hate, but not enough to make us love one another.
Diligence is the mother of good fortune, and idleness, its opposite, never brought a man to the goal of any of his best wishes.
It is no use to blame the looking glass if your face is awry.

If you would have your son to walk honourably through the world, you must not attempt to clear the stones from his path, but teach him to walk firmly over them—not insist upon leading him by the hand, but let him learn to go alone.
The world is charged with the grandeur of God.
In every adversity of fortune, to have been happy is the most unhappy kind of misfortune.
He that is down needs fear no fall.
Nature is not a temple, but a workshop, and man is the workman in it.
Do not block the way of inquiry.
Laws are always unstable unless they are founded on the manners of a nation; and manners are the only durable and resisting power in a people.
Everyone sees what you appear to be, few experience what you really are.
I’m not afraid of storms, for I’m learning how to sail my ship.
We hold these truths to be self-evident: that all men and women are created equal.
Water, water, every where, nor any drop to drink.
quotes.source: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner (1798)

quotes.t: I, too, sing America.

A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.bio: Indian aerospace scientist and the 11th President of India (2002-2007), known as the 'Missile Man of India'.

Albert Camus.bio: French-Algerian writer and philosopher, author of The Stranger; Nobel Prize in Literature 1957.

Albert Schweitzer.bio: Albert Schweitzer was an Alsatian theologian, musician and physician who founded a hospital at Lambaréné in Gabon and served there for decades. His philosophy of reverence for life and his Bach scholarship earned him the Nobel Peace Prize in 1952.

Alexis de Tocqueville.bio: French political thinker and historian most famous for Democracy in America.

Anais Nin.bio: Anaïs Nin, French-born American diarist and novelist. She is celebrated for her multi-volume Diary, begun when she was eleven, and for works such as Delta of Venus.

Anne Brontë.bio: English novelist and poet, youngest of the Brontë siblings, author of Agnes Grey and The Tenant of Wildfell Hall.

Anne Frank.bio: German-born Jewish diarist whose diary documents life in hiding during the Holocaust.

Benjamin Disraeli.bio: British statesman who served twice as Prime Minister and led the Conservative Party. He was also a successful novelist, writing books such as Coningsby and Sybil.
Benjamin Disraeli.credit: Cornelius Jabez Hughes, Public domain (File: File:Benjamin Disraeli, Earl of Beaconsfield.jpg)

Benjamin Franklin.bio: American polymath - printer, scientist, diplomat - and a Founding Father of the United States.

Blaise Pascal.bio: French mathematician, physicist and philosopher, author of the Pensées.
Blaise Pascal.credit: unknown; a copy of the painting of François II Quesnel, which was made for Gérard Edelinck en 1691, Public domain

Boethius.bio: Roman Christian philosopher, poet and politician who wrote The Consolation of Philosophy while imprisoned.

Carl Jung.bio: Swiss psychiatrist who founded analytical psychology. His concepts of the collective unconscious, archetypes and introversion and extraversion remain influential in psychology and culture.
Carl Jung.credit: AnonymousUnknown author, Public domain (File: File:CARL JUNG (1875 - 1961).jpg)

Charles Dickens.bio: English novelist and social critic; author of A Christmas Carol, Oliver Twist and Great Expectations.

Charles Sanders Peirce.bio: American philosopher, logician, mathematician and scientist regarded as a founder of pragmatism.

Desmond Tutu.bio: South African Anglican archbishop and Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1984) who campaigned against apartheid.

Dogen.bio: Founder of the Sōtō school of Zen in Japan and author of the Shōbōgenzō, a landmark of Buddhist philosophy.

Eleanor Roosevelt.bio: Eleanor Roosevelt was the longest-serving First Lady of the United States, from 1933 to 1945, and reinvented the role as a platform for civil rights and social reform. Afterward she became a US delegate to the United Nations and chaired the commission that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
Eleanor Roosevelt.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author, Public domain (File: Eleanor Roosevelt portrait 1933.jpg)

Elizabeth Cady Stanton.bio: American social activist who helped organise the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention, the first women's rights convention.

Emily Dickinson.bio: American poet whose nearly 1,800 poems, mostly unpublished in her lifetime, made her a central figure of American literature.
Emily Dickinson.credit: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress, Public domain

Friedrich Nietzsche.bio: German philosopher known for Thus Spoke Zarathustra and the concept of the will to power.

Fyodor Dostoevsky.bio: Russian novelist, author of Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov.

George Bernard Shaw.bio: Irish playwright and critic; author of Pygmalion; Nobel Prize in Literature 1925.
George Bernard Shaw.credit: Sussman, Public domain (File: George Bernard Shaw, playwright (SAYRE 9001).jpg)

Gerard Manley Hopkins.bio: English Jesuit priest and poet whose poems were published posthumously in 1918.

Helen Keller.bio: American author and activist who, deaf and blind from childhood, became a renowned advocate for disability rights.
Helen Keller.credit: Los Angeles Times; restored by User:Rhododendrites, Public domain

Henry David Thoreau.bio: American writer known for Walden (1854) and the essay Civil Disobedience.

Ivan Turgenev.bio: Russian novelist whose Fathers and Sons (1862) is a landmark of Russian realism.

Jane Austen.bio: English novelist known for Pride and Prejudice and Emma, celebrated for irony and social observation.
Jane Austen.credit: Engraving by William Home Lizars after James Andrews, Public domain

Jawaharlal Nehru.bio: Leader of India's independence movement and the country's first Prime Minister (1947-1964).

John Bunyan.bio: English Christian writer and preacher best known for The Pilgrim’s Progress.

John Lennon.bio: English singer-songwriter, co-founder of the Beatles and solo artist known for Imagine.

Jonathan Swift.bio: Anglo-Irish writer and satirist, author of Thoughts on Various Subjects.

Langston Hughes.bio: American poet and a leading figure of the Harlem Renaissance.

Leo Tolstoy.bio: Russian novelist, author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina.

Leonardo da Vinci.bio: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian Renaissance painter, engineer and anatomist whose notebooks reveal an insatiable curiosity about nature and art. He painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, and filled thousands of pages with studies, inventions and observations.
Leonardo da Vinci.credit: Leonardo da Vinci, Public domain (File: Leonardo self.jpg)

Louisa May Alcott.bio: American novelist best known for Little Women (1868).

Mahatma Gandhi.bio: Leader of India's nonviolent independence movement; pioneered satyagraha and became the father of the Indian nation.

Martin Luther King Jr..bio: American Baptist minister who led the civil rights movement; Nobel Peace Prize laureate 1964.

Maya Angelou.bio: American poet and memoirist best known for I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings (1969).
Maya Angelou.credit: Bee Photos by Ryan Marty, Public domain

Miguel de Cervantes.bio: Spanish novelist, poet and playwright best known for Don Quixote.

Miyamoto Musashi.bio: Legendary Japanese swordsman, undefeated in over sixty duels, author of The Book of Five Rings and the Dokkodo.

Mother Teresa.bio: Albanian-Indian Catholic nun who founded the Missionaries of Charity in Kolkata; Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1979).
Mother Teresa.credit: John Mathew Smith & www.celebrity-photos.com from Laurel  Maryland, USA, CC BY-SA 2.0

Napoleon Bonaparte.bio: Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution and became Emperor of the French in 1804. His Napoleonic Wars reshaped Europe, and his Napoleonic Code influenced legal systems worldwide. He died in exile on Saint Helena.

Nelson Mandela.role: Anti-apartheid leader, President of South Africa
Nelson Mandela.bio: South African anti-apartheid revolutionary who spent 27 years in prison and became the country's first Black president in 1994.

Niccolò Machiavelli.bio: Niccolò Machiavelli was a Florentine diplomat and writer whose treatise The Prince analysed power with unsentimental realism. Long read as a manual of cunning statecraft, his works also include discourses defending republican government.

Nikolai Gogol.bio: Ukrainian-born Russian writer best known for Dead Souls and The Government Inspector.

Oprah Winfrey.bio: American talk-show host and media executive whose long-running show made her one of the most influential broadcasters in history.
Oprah Winfrey.credit: US Embassy South Africa, Public domain

Oscar Wilde.bio: Irish playwright, poet and author of The Picture of Dorian Gray, famed for his wit and epigrams.
Oscar Wilde.credit: Napoleon Sarony (restoration by Adam Cuerden), Public domain

Pablo Picasso.bio: Pablo Picasso was a Spanish artist who co-founded Cubism and reinvented his style across a career of nearly eighty years. Works such as Les Demoiselles d'Avignon and Guernica made him the most famous and influential artist of the 20th century.
Pablo Picasso.credit: Didier Descouens, Public domain (File: File:(Barcelona) Retrat de Picasso - Pablo Gargallo - Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalunya.jpg)

Pema Chodron.bio: Pema Chodron is an American nun in the Tibetan Buddhist tradition and a widely read author and teacher. Her books, including When Things Fall Apart, bring Buddhist teachings on compassion and difficulty to a broad audience.

Plato.bio: Greek philosopher, student of Socrates and author of The Republic.

Samuel Taylor Coleridge.bio: Samuel Taylor Coleridge was an English poet and critic, a founder of the Romantic movement alongside William Wordsworth. His poems include 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner' and 'Kubla Khan', and his Biographia Literaria is a landmark of literary criticism.

Socrates.bio: Greek philosopher of Athens, central figure of Western philosophy; left no writings.

Sophocles.bio: Sophocles was an Athenian tragedian who wrote more than 120 plays, of which seven survive complete. Oedipus Rex and Antigone, his most famous works, set the pattern for Western tragedy.

Sun Tzu.bio: Ancient Chinese general traditionally credited with The Art of War, a treatise on strategy studied worldwide for over two thousand years.
Sun Tzu.credit: Unknown author, Public domain (File: 吴司马孙武.jpg)

Swami Vivekananda.bio: Indian Hindu monk who introduced Vedanta and Yoga to the West; famous for his 1893 Chicago Parliament of Religions address.
Swami Vivekananda.credit: Unknown author, Public domain (File: Swami Vivekananda at Parliament of Religions.jpg)

Tony Robbins.bio: Tony Robbins is an American author, coach and motivational speaker known for bestselling books such as Unlimited Power and Awaken the Giant Within. His seminars and self-help programmes have made him one of the most prominent figures in the personal development industry.

Victor Hugo.bio: French poet and novelist, author of Les Misérables and The Hunchback of Notre-Dame.
Victor Hugo.credit: Étienne Carjat, Public domain (File: Victor Hugo by Étienne Carjat 1876 - full.jpg)

Voltaire.bio: Voltaire, born François-Marie Arouet, was a French Enlightenment writer, philosopher and historian famous for the novella Candide and for his witty defence of civil liberties, including freedom of speech and religion. He was one of the most prolific and influential writers of his age.

Winston Churchill.bio: British prime minister during the Second World War and Nobel laureate in Literature.
